headline: AI-generated menus suffer from a 'sameness problem', creating unappetizing, eerily flawless food images
summary: AI models trained on narrow "pleasing" aesthetics are producing food menus that look unsettlingly perfect and homogenous. This "convergence" degrades quality without making the AI useless.
details: Many cafes and restaurants are now using AI-generated menu illustrations that appear eerily flawless and precisely symmetrical, often eliciting a visceral feeling that something is wrong. These images can range from subtly off to egregiously fake, like a burrito with impossibly bubbly cheese.

This phenomenon stems from generative AI models trained on a narrow, "pleasing" aesthetic. Reality Defender CTO Alex Lisle describes it as "an alien trying to make a pizza without understanding its core principles," leading to "Lovecraftian food horrors."

AI models, like LLMs and diffusion models, learn patterns from vast datasets to generate images. Lisle notes that many AI-generated food images resemble "a Chili’s menu from 2015" because that style formed a significant part of their training corpus.

A critical issue arises when AI models inadvertently train on too much of their own AI-generated content, risking "model collapse." While not full collapse, the current "convergence" degrades output quality, making images homogenous and less authentic.

The optimization of datasets for "pleasingness" or "not being offensive" leads to this homogenization, effectively "shaving off the edges" of variety and realism. This process makes AI-generated food look increasingly artificial and uncomfortable.

An X user, Labtec, demonstrated this by editing an AI-generated menu 100 times, showing how food items progressively lost their natural appearance. The experiment revealed how repeated AI generation and editing can lead to unsettlingly unnatural results.

headline_marked: [[Apple sued for $2.7 billion]] over App Tracking Transparency rules
headline: Apple sued for $2.7 billion over App Tracking Transparency rules
summary: Apple faces a £2 billion ($2.7 billion) lawsuit in the UK. A former antitrust official claims its App Tracking Transparency policy unfairly favors Apple's own advertising ecosystem over third-party developers.
details: Apple is facing a £2 billion ($2.7 billion) lawsuit in the UK over its App Tracking Transparency (ATT) policy. The suit, filed by a former UK antitrust official on behalf of app developers, alleges that Apple applies stricter rules to third-party developers than to its own services, giving its advertising ecosystem an unfair advantage.

ATT, launched in 2021, was designed to give users more control over app tracking across websites and other apps. Apple has stated it is "bound by the exact same requirements as all developers" under the policy.

However, regulators in several European countries, including France, Italy, and Poland, have investigated ATT. Germany's Federal Cartel Office recently found that Apple's ATT pop-ups could encourage consent for its own services while discouraging it for third-party apps.

Following these findings, Apple agreed to implement changes to how ATT functions within the European Union. This comes after the French Competition Authority previously fined Apple €150 million ($175 million) over ATT last year.
